name: Toupouri (Dziguilao)
overview: In the majority in their area, the Toupouri, long very isolated, now live alongside the Fulani and Moundang. Having come from Sudan through Chad, with which they live “in absolute fraternity”, they organise their society around the doore (land chiefs), clan notables and maagay initiates. Farming, livestock, bil-bil and pottery are their livelihood, and the cockerel festival, the feo kake, opens the new year every October.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Majority group, formerly very isolated, now mixed with the Fulani (notably in Guidiguis) and neighbouring the Moundang.
Toupouri is spoken in Chad and, in Cameroon, as far as Touboro, Nkoteng and Mbandjock.
Largely indigenous and endogamous group; the men, who are more mobile, marry outside more often.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: Ancestral land “conquered at the price of blood”.
Having come from Sudan via Chad, they have lost the link with Sudan but remain very close to the Toupouri of Chad.
Relations with neighbours have known tensions (land, circumcision, memories of conquest).

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: The wandoore (in Chad) and the doore govern; the notables are the heads of neighbourhoods and clans (three in Dziguilao); the blacksmiths form a caste, the moungouri.
Decisions are taken by consensus between the doore and the notables.
You do not marry within your own clan; in-laws may joke with one another, by virtue of the alliance.
The maagay lead the initiation.
The woman bows or kneels before handing over water or any object.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the young woman joins her husband.
The boy becomes a man at around 18 (build, deep voice); the girl at around 15, with puberty.
Formerly, many cattle were needed and the husband was imposed on young girls; today, they choose and the bride price is adapted.
Steps: choice of the young girl, request, handing over of the “water money” that opens the engagement (to clothe and honour the fiancée), bride price in cattle or goats, with a spear.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: Cults: the feo kake, the cockerel festival, in October at the start of the harvests and of the new year; the moungouri festival; the sacred djatobe tree.
Sacred places marked by trees: Djaksiri (sacred land), Koumaijwa, Padde, Guirsay, Bobio, Wersore, Dziguilao.
The child is a gift from God; the father offers ox feet for the mother's broth. Death takes one back to the forebears, who make themselves known through dreams and rituals.
Taboos: talking about initiation, incest; prohibitions: adultery, striking one's elders (uncles, aunts).
Divination by eggs, water, the mirror; there are oracles (halgue, djarkounene).

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Men: farming, livestock rearing, trade. Women: farming, pottery, selling bil-bil.
The land belongs to the men; one inherits from one's father or clears one's own space.
Ancestral crafts: clay pots for the home and for sale, hats against the sun.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: Formerly, a skin loincloth, cotton weaving, clothes made of leaves.
Traditional medicine retains a certain vitality, without curing everything.
Beauty: the man with a thick beard and moustache, of medium height and build; the woman of medium height, with thick eyebrows and hair.
Courtship: glances, attire, gait; the woman may offer kola nut to the man.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Dances: gourna and waywa (mixed), dilna and siila (men), wiile (women), doundouloun.
Instruments: tam-tam (mangoura), flute, stick, spear, hook, guitar.
Festival: the feo kake (cockerel festival), every year in October.

sections.title: History and cultural kinship
items: Tchaossala, the oldest ancestor cited, was a figure of resistance to the Fulani conquests.
The Toupouri share traits with the Moundang and the Gbaya.

sections.title: The names
items: May- marks women's names, Pa- or Wa- men's.
The name is given according to the circumstances, sometimes revealed in a dream; it changes once, at initiation.
Everyone is called by their own name.

lessons.title: Who are the Toupouri (Dziguilao)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Toupouri (Dziguilao) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Toupouri (Dziguilao) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Toupouri (Dziguilao) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Toupouri (Dziguilao) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Toupouri (Dziguilao) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Toupouri (Dziguilao) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Majority group, once very isolated, today mixed with the Fulani (notably at Guidiguis) and neighbouring the Moundang. • Toupouri is spoken in Chad and, in Cameroon, as far as Touboro, Nkoteng and Mbandjock. • Largely native and endogamous group; men, being more mobile, marry outside more often. • Ancestral land “won at the price of blood”. • Coming from Sudan through Chad, they have lost the link with Sudan but remain very close to the Toupouri of Chad.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: In the majority in their area, the Toupouri, long very isolated, now live alongside the Fulani and Moundang. Having come from Sudan through Chad, with which they live “in absolute fraternity”, they organise their society around the doore (land chiefs), clan notables and maagay initiates. Farming, livestock, bil-bil and pottery are their livelihood, and the cockerel festival, the feo kake, opens the new year every October.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Toupouri (Dziguilao) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

objectives: Linking food to the living environment

vocabulary.langText: couscous de mil rouge et jaune

lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Toupouri (Dziguilao), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Toupouri (Dziguilao).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Toupouri (Dziguilao), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Toupouri (Dziguilao).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: red and yellow millet couscous, bay chèrè and tchenglèrè sauces, baobab leaves (konkon), beef and goat meat. • Drinks: bil-bil, arki. • Men: farming, livestock rearing, trade. Women: farming, pottery, selling bil-bil.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Toupouri (Dziguilao) eat mainly red and yellow millet couscous, bay chèrè and tchenglèrè sauces, baobab leaves, beef and goat meat. Traditional drinks: bil-bil, arki. These foods are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Toupouri (Dziguilao)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Toupouri (Dziguilao), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Toupouri (Dziguilao). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Toupouri (Dziguilao), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Toupouri (Dziguilao)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death
lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Toupouri (Dziguilao), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Toupouri (Dziguilao). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Toupouri (Dziguilao), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Toupouri (Dziguilao). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • Cults: the feo kake, the cockerel festival, in October at the start of the harvests and of the new year; the festival of the moungouri; the sacred djatobe tree. • Sacred places marked by trees: Djaksiri (sacred land), Koumaijwa, Padde, Guirsay, Bobio, Wersore, Dziguilao. • The child is a gift from God; the father offers cattle trotters for the mother's broth. Death takes one back to the ancestors, who make themselves known through dreams and rituals. • Taboos: talking about initiation, incest; prohibitions: adultery, striking one's elders (uncles, aunts). • Divination with eggs, water, the mirror; there are oracles (halgue, djarkounene).

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Cults: the feo kake, the rooster festival, held in October at the start of the harvest and of the new year; the moungouri festival; the sacred djatobe tree. Sacred places marked by trees: Djaksiri (sacred land), Koumaijwa, Padde, Guirsay, Bobio, Wersore, Dziguilao.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Toupouri (Dziguilao) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Toupouri
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day

vocabulary.frenchText: morning greetings (as a sign of deference/respect)

lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Toupouri (Dziguilao) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Toupouri (Dziguilao) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Toupouri (Dziguilao) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Toupouri (Dziguilao) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following elements, or have the students discover them: • The language of the community is Toupouri. • Greeting formulas: Ine/ Lla = Hello (neutral formula, at any time); Ndo nayaola/Ndo naawé = morning greeting (one person); Ndo nayaola/Ndo naawé = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Bong, Bogè, Swa’a, Naa, Dwee. • Everyone is called by their own name. • Tchaossala, the oldest ancestor mentioned, was a figure of resistance to the Fulani conquests.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Toupouri are the first steps towards communicating with the Toupouri (Dziguilao). Polite formulas express the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.
